cosponsors: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

steps.intent: Estonia's primary objective is to firmly establish climate-related security risks within the Security Council's conflict prevention and peacekeeping architecture through systematic reporting by the Secretary-General. The most difficult challenge is overcoming fierce resistance from the Russian Federation and China, who argue that climate change belongs exclusively under the UNFCCC framework rather than the Security Council's Chapter VII purview. We also anticipate substantial pushback regarding sovereignty, mission creep, and the prospect of a Russian veto against any thematic, legally binding Council mandate on this issue.

messages.China: China emphasizes that the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement remain the primary and authoritative multilateral frameworks for addressing climate change, guided by the fundamental principle of common but differentiated responsibilities. The Security Council lacks specialized expertise and tools in this domain, and establishing a generic, thematic mechanism risks duplicating efforts and encroaching upon the mandates of the General Assembly, ECOSOC, and the UNFCCC. Any Council engagement must strictly adhere to country-specific contexts already on our agenda and respect the division of labor across the United Nations system.
messages.France: France fully supports this historic draft resolution, which addresses one of the defining challenges of our time. As the adverse effects of climate change act as an undeniable threat multiplier for instability and conflict—most notably in regions like the Sahel and Lake Chad—the Security Council must equip the UN system with the tools to integrate climate-related security risks into conflict prevention and peacekeeping. We commend the penholders for their consultative approach and urge all Council members to adopt this text without delay.
messages.India: India firmly opposes attempts to bring climate change under the mandate of the Security Council, which lacks the universal representation and technical expertise required to address this complex development issue. Securitizing climate action undermines the established multilateral architecture under the UNFCCC and dilutes the foundational principles of equity and Common But Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR-RC). We cannot support a generic thematic resolution that creates a parallel track and institutionalizes Council oversight over global climate action.
messages.Ireland: Ireland strongly supports the draft resolution in its current form and is proud to co-sponsor this historic initiative. The text strikes a careful and necessary balance, establishing a concrete framework for the Council to address climate-related security risks without encroaching upon the mandate of the UNFCCC. We urge all Council members to join the broad cross-regional coalition of co-sponsors and adopt this text without dilution.
messages.Kenya: Kenya strongly supports this resolution, as the adverse impacts of climate change are already aggravating conflicts, displacement, and resource competition across Africa, notably in the Horn of Africa and the Sahel. To ensure operational effectiveness, the Council must explicitly leverage partnerships with regional and sub-regional mechanisms, such as the African Union and IGAD, and uphold national ownership. We stand ready to work with the penholders to secure the adoption of this critical framework.
messages.Mexico: Mexico proudly co-sponsors this draft resolution, which reflects an urgent and balanced response to the clear links between climate change, fragility, and conflict. The text properly recognizes the UNFCCC as the primary forum for climate action while equipping the Security Council with essential reporting and analytical tools to prevent conflict. We fully support the draft as currently formulated and urge its swift adoption without dilution.
messages.Niger: As a co-penholder and a nation directly facing the destabilizing security consequences of environmental degradation and climate change in the Sahel and Lake Chad basin, Niger fully endorses this draft resolution. Integrating climate-related security risks into UN conflict-prevention strategies and peacekeeping mandates is vital for safeguarding international peace and security. We strongly urge all Council members to rally behind this balanced and essential text.
messages.Norway: Norway fully supports the draft resolution as tabled and is proud to be among its co-sponsors. Addressing climate-related security risks is a key priority for Norway and an indispensable responsibility of the Security Council in maintaining international peace and security. We strongly commend the penholders for crafting a balanced text and urge all Council members to adopt this historic resolution.
messages.Russian Federation: The Russian Federation cannot accept the securitization of the climate agenda, which properly belongs within the purview of the UNFCCC, ECOSOC, and the General Assembly. Attempting to establish a generic, automatic link between climate change and international security ignores the genuine political, social, and economic root causes of conflicts and infringes upon national sovereignty. We strongly advise against forcing a divisive thematic draft resolution onto the Security Council, which lacks both the specialized mandate and expertise to address global environmental issues.
messages.Saint Vincent and the Grenadines: As a co-sponsor and a Small Island Developing State on the frontline of the climate crisis, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines strongly supports this landmark draft resolution. For SIDS and fragile regions across the globe, climate change is an existential threat and a clear multiplier of insecurity and instability that the Security Council cannot ignore. We urge all Council members to support this balanced and necessary text.
messages.Tunisia: As a co-sponsor of this draft resolution, Tunisia fully supports the text as currently drafted, reflecting a balanced and essential recognition of climate change as an aggravating factor for instability and conflict, particularly in Africa and the Arab region. We commend the leadership of our fellow A3 member Niger alongside Ireland and Estonia in stewarding this vital initiative through transparent and broad consultations. We believe the draft properly respects the primacy of the UNFCCC while equipping the Council and United Nations peace operations with necessary tools to assess and mitigate climate-related security risks.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom strongly supports this landmark draft resolution and is proud to co-sponsor it. Having just hosted COP26 in Glasgow and championed the climate and security agenda in this Council since 2007, the UK firmly believes that addressing climate-related security risks is integral to conflict prevention and maintaining international peace and security. We urge all Council members to unite behind this balanced, timely, and urgently needed text.
messages.United States of America: The United States is proud to co-sponsor this landmark resolution and fully supports the text as drafted. The climate crisis is an undeniable reality and an acute threat multiplier that directly impacts international peace and security. Integrating climate-related security risks into the Council's conflict-prevention strategies and reporting is long overdue, and we urge all Council members to join the overwhelming majority of the UN membership in voting in favor.
messages.Viet Nam: As one of the countries most severely affected by climate change, Viet Nam strongly supports international efforts to address climate-related security risks and welcomes this initiative. We emphasize that the Council's role must remain focused on country-specific situations on its agenda while fully respecting national sovereignty and the primary role of the UNFCCC in global climate governance. We encourage the co-sponsors to accommodate constructive proposals from all members to ensure broad Council consensus.

steps.summary: Estonia has preserved the core operational provisions of the draft—specifically regular dedicated reporting by the Secretary-General and the integration of climate-related security risks into conflict prevention and peacekeeping mandates. To broaden ownership and bridge divides, the revision incorporates the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities (CBDR-RC) in PP3, strengthens partnerships with regional organizations and host States (Kenya, Viet Nam), and clarifies the primary mandates of specialized UN bodies (China). Outright deletions of the operative core sought by Russia and India were rejected to protect the fundamental purpose of this landmark resolution.

messages.China: China appreciates the inclusion of the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities in the preambular text. However, we remain deeply concerned by attempts to establish a generic thematic mandate and recurring reporting mechanism for the Security Council on climate change, which risks duplicating the work of and encroaching upon the specialized mandates of the UNFCCC, ECOSOC, and the General Assembly. The Council should focus strictly on country-specific situations where climate factors exacerbate existing conflicts, rather than over-securitizing global climate governance.
messages.France: France fully supports this balanced and timely draft resolution, which reflects the clear link between climate disruption and international security. Climate change is a proven threat multiplier, particularly in fragile regions such as the Sahel, and the Security Council cannot remain silent on these challenges. We commend the penholders for maintaining high ambition while appropriately recognizing the primacy of the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement, and we urge all Council members to vote in favor.
messages.India: India maintains its principled position that the Security Council is not the appropriate forum to address climate change, which must remain under the consensus-driven framework of the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement. Attempting to securitize climate action and establish institutional reporting and operational mandates within the Council undermines the multilateral architecture and sidesteps foundational principles like Common But Differentiated Responsibilities. As our fundamental concerns regarding the Council's encroachment onto this subject matter remain unaddressed, India cannot support this text.
messages.Ireland: Ireland strongly supports this landmark draft resolution and is proud to be among its co-sponsors. The current text strikes a vital balance by integrating climate-related security risks into conflict prevention and Council reporting while fully respecting the primacy of the UNFCCC and the principle of national ownership. We urge fellow Council members to maintain the integrity of these core provisions and look forward to voting in favor of its adoption.
messages.Kenya: Kenya thanks the co-penholders for incorporating our proposals emphasizing the role of regional and sub-regional organizations as well as consultation with host States. The revised text effectively captures the link between climate change, fragility, and conflict while respecting the primacy of the UNFCCC and national ownership. Kenya fully supports this draft resolution and looks forward to voting in favor.
messages.Mexico: As a proud co-sponsor of this draft resolution, Mexico fully supports the current text without reservations. The draft strikes an essential balance by recognizing climate change as an aggravating risk factor for international peace and security while fully respecting the primacy of the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement. We commend the penholders for their inclusive consultations and urge the Council to adopt this historic resolution.
messages.Niger: Niger expresses its full and resolute support for the draft resolution as currently formulated. For our region, the Sahel and the Lake Chad basin, climate change is an immediate reality that exacerbates conflict, displaces communities, and fuels violent extremism. This balanced text provides the United Nations with the essential analytical and operational tools to address climate-related security risks, and we urge all Council members to vote in favor.
messages.Norway: Norway is a proud co-sponsor of this landmark draft resolution and fully supports the text as presented. Addressing climate-related security risks is a key priority for our Council tenure, and this draft strikes the right balance by strengthening the UN's conflict prevention architecture while fully respecting the UNFCCC framework and national ownership. We urge all Council members to support this vital initiative.
messages.Russian Federation: The Russian Federation firmly opposes attempts to artificially link climate change to the Security Council's agenda and securitize an issue that belongs squarely within the mandate of specialized bodies like the UNFCCC and the General Assembly. Establishing generic reporting obligations and integrating climate risks into Council conflict-prevention mandates encroaches upon the division of labor within the United Nations and ignores the genuine socioeconomic drivers of conflict. If the penholder proceeds with these unacceptable provisions, Russia will not be able to support this draft resolution.
messages.Saint Vincent and the Grenadines: As a co-sponsor and a Small Island Developing State on the frontlines of the climate crisis, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines fully supports the draft resolution as written. The text strikes a necessary and carefully crafted balance, reaffirming the primary role of the UNFCCC while rightly empowering the United Nations system to systematically address the acute security risks and threat-multiplying impacts of climate change. We urge all Council members to support this vital and timely initiative.
messages.Tunisia: Tunisia reaffirms its full support for this draft resolution as a proud co-sponsor. We commend the penholders for presenting a well-balanced text that properly underscores the adverse impacts of climate change on stability and conflict prevention, particularly across Africa and the Arab region, while fully respecting the UNFCCC framework and national sovereignty. We stand ready to vote in favor of this important initiative.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom fully supports this draft resolution and is proud to be among its co-sponsors. Addressing climate-related security risks is essential to the Council's core mandate of maintaining international peace and security and preventing conflict. We commend the penholders for bringing forward a balanced, forward-looking text that reflects the overwhelming call from the wider UN membership, and we look forward to voting in favor.
messages.United States of America: The United States is proud to co-sponsor this landmark draft resolution, which reflects the clear view of a vast majority of the UN membership that climate change is an urgent threat multiplier for global peace and security. The current text strikes a careful balance, respecting the UNFCCC's primacy while equipping the Security Council and UN peace operations with the analytical tools needed to address climate-related security risks. We urge all members of the Council to vote in favor of this critical and overdue resolution.
messages.Viet Nam: Viet Nam thanks the penholders for constructively incorporating our key priorities into the revised draft, particularly the reaffirmation of the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities, national ownership, and respect for the primary mandates of the UNFCCC and specialized UN bodies. As a country acutely vulnerable to the impacts of climate change, Viet Nam believes this draft provides a balanced, context-sensitive framework for addressing climate-related security risks while upholding the UN Charter. steps.summary: Estonia maintains the integrity of the draft resolution alongside the broad cross-regional coalition of co-sponsors and Council members who view climate change as a critical threat multiplier. Acceding to the demands of the Russian Federation and India to delete the core conflict-prevention and dedicated reporting mandates would fundamentally hollow out the text and disregard the clear call of the vast majority of the UN membership. The draft resolution is therefore submitted to the Council for a vote in its current balanced form.

before.Ireland:
Ireland is proud to co-sponsor this landmark draft resolution alongside Niger and over one hundred UN Member States from across every region of the world. 

For Ireland, and for the vast majority of the international community, the link between climate change and international peace and security is an undeniable reality. From the Sahel to the Horn of Africa, to small island developing states, we see every day how climate-induced shocks, resource scarcity, and extreme weather act as risk multipliers—aggravating vulnerabilities, displacing populations, and fueling instability and conflict. 

This resolution does not seek to duplicate or encroach upon the vital work of the UNFCCC. Rather, it asks the Security Council to face up to its core responsibility under the UN Charter. It provides the Council, UN peace operations, and the Secretary-General with the essential tools, evidence-based reporting, and analysis needed to understand and address climate-related security risks, enabling more effective conflict prevention and peacebuilding. 

The overwhelming support across the General Assembly membership demonstrates that the time for this Council to act is now. We urge all members of the Council to vote in favour of this historic resolution.
before.Niger:
Niger, together with Ireland, had the honor of co-sponsoring and presenting this draft resolution, which reflects the undeniable reality faced daily by the peoples of the Sahel, Lake Chad, and fragile regions across the world. For our countries, the link between climate change, desertification, resource scarcity, and insecurity is not a theoretical debate or an academic concept; it is an existential, lived reality that fuels intercommunal conflict and provides fertile ground for terrorist and armed groups.

This draft resolution does not seek to supplant the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, nor does it encroach upon the development prerogatives of other United Nations organs. Rather, it equips the Security Council and the United Nations system with the analytical tools and context-specific reporting necessary to anticipate, mitigate, and respond to the security implications of climate disruption where they directly threaten peace and stability. 

Over 110 Member States have co-sponsored this historic initiative, demonstrating a clear and resounding call from the international community. We urge all members of the Security Council to shoulder their Charter responsibilities, listen to the voices of affected regions, and vote overwhelmingly in favor of this draft resolution.
before.Russian Federation:
The Russian Federation will vote against the draft resolution submitted to the Council today. 

Our position of principle is well known: we share the international community's profound concern over the global challenge of climate change. However, addressing this issue requires a specialized, scientific, and depoliticized approach within the established international platforms, primarily the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and the Paris Agreement, which operate on the basis of consensus and respect for the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities. 

Attempting to introduce an automatic link between climate change and international security into the Security Council is counterproductive and fundamentally flawed. The Council lacks the expertise, tools, and mandate to address socio-economic and environmental issues. Furthermore, creating a generic, one-size-fits-all approach ignores the true, specific, and multifaceted drivers of conflicts, which are predominantly political, economic, and social. Instead of fostering genuine international cooperation, this initiative seeks to establish a pretext for Council encroachment into the domestic affairs of sovereign States and to divert resources and attention away from the genuine root causes of instability.

Our fundamental concerns and red lines were entirely disregarded by the sponsors, who chose a divisive path of confrontation over consensus. Under these circumstances, the Russian Federation cannot support this text and will vote against it.

after.China:
China attaches great importance to addressing climate change and is firmly committed to green, low-carbon, and sustainable development. We are actively implementing our national strategy to tackle climate change, have set ambitious carbon peak and carbon neutrality targets, and are making vigorous efforts to promote international cooperation under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and the Paris Agreement. We fully understand and share the profound concerns of developing countries, in particular small island developing States and African countries, regarding the severe challenges posed by climate change to their survival and development.

At the same time, China’s position on the draft resolution before us is clear and consistent. Climate change is, in essence, an issue of sustainable development. The international community already has dedicated, authoritative platforms to address it, namely the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement. These mechanisms operate on the basis of universal participation, scientific assessment, and broad consensus, upholding the bedrock principle of common but differentiated responsibilities. 

The Security Council is not a specialized body on environmental or development issues. It lacks the professional expertise, operational tools, and representation to effectively manage global climate governance. Establishing a direct and generalized link between climate change and peace and security risks encroaching upon the mandates of specialized UN bodies and multilateral processes, while diverting attention away from the core issues of climate mitigation, adaptation, and finance. What developing countries urgently need is not empty rhetoric or securitized concepts, but concrete financial support, technology transfer, and capacity-building. In particular, developed countries must fulfill their long-overdue commitment of providing 100 billion US dollars annually in climate finance.

Any meaningful action by the Security Council on global challenges must be based on broad consensus among Member States. Regrettably, despite persistent, serious differences of view among Council members and the wider UN membership, the co-sponsors chose to force a vote on this draft resolution. Such an approach does not foster unity or address the real concerns of developing countries. For these reasons, China abstained in the vote on the draft resolution.

China remains ready to work with all parties to advance international cooperation on climate change through the appropriate channels, promote the full and effective implementation of the Paris Agreement, and support developing countries in achieving green recovery and sustainable development.
after.Estonia:
Mr. President,

Estonia expresses its deep regret and profound disappointment that the Security Council was unable to adopt this historic draft resolution today, solely due to the veto of one permanent member. 

We would like to express our sincere appreciation to Ireland and Niger for their outstanding leadership, dedication, and tireless efforts in preparing this balanced, inclusive, and timely text. We also thank the 113 co-sponsors from all regions of the world—one of the highest numbers of co-sponsors in the history of the Security Council—demonstrating the overwhelming support and urgent demand across the United Nations membership for Council action on this critical issue.

For Estonia, the link between climate change and international peace and security is clear and undeniable. Climate change is a reality that is already destabilizing communities, exacerbating competition over scarce resources, fueling displacement, and compounding existing vulnerabilities and conflicts, particularly in fragile regions such as the Sahel, the Lake Chad Basin, and the Horn of Africa, as well as for small island developing States. It acts as an undisputable risk and threat multiplier.

The draft resolution put before us today did not seek to duplicate the work of specialized environmental bodies like the UNFCCC. Instead, it was an effort to equip the United Nations system and this Council with the analytical tools, reporting, and context-specific information necessary to fulfill our core mandate: the maintenance of international peace and security and the prevention of conflict. 

By failing to adopt this resolution today, the Council has missed a vital opportunity to address one of the defining security challenges of our time. It is unacceptable that the Council has been prevented from responding to the clear call of the vast majority of UN Member States and the vulnerable populations most affected by climate-induced insecurity.

Despite today’s outcome, the reality on the ground will not change, nor will the urgency of addressing climate-related security risks disappear. Estonia remains steadfast in its commitment to advancing the climate and security agenda, and we will continue to work closely with our partners across the United Nations to build resilience, prevent conflict, and ensure that our multilateral response reflects today’s complex security environment.

Thank you, Mr. President.
after.France:
France deeply regrets the result of today’s vote and, in particular, the use of the veto by the Russian Federation, which has prevented the Security Council from adopting a landmark resolution supported by the vast majority of United Nations Member States.

France voted in favour of this text, which was co-sponsored by 113 States from every region of the world. We warmly commend Ireland and Niger for their tireless and transparent efforts as penholders to build a balanced, constructive, and forward-looking text.

The reality before us is undeniable: climate change is not merely an environmental or development challenge; it is an existential threat and a powerful multiplier of instability, conflict, and human suffering. We see its destabilizing effects every day, particularly in the Sahel, the Lake Chad basin, the Horn of Africa, and across vulnerable small island developing states. Droughts, desertification, and competition over scarce water and arable land fuel tensions between communities and create fertile ground for armed groups and terrorist organizations.

Addressing the security impacts of climate change does not in any way encroach upon the vital work of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change or the Paris Agreement, which remain the primary negotiating forums. Rather, this draft resolution sought to provide the United Nations system and this Council with the analytical tools and regular reporting necessary to understand, anticipate, and respond effectively to climate-related security risks, particularly in peace operations. 

By paralyzing the Council today, the veto does not make the reality of climate change disappear. It only prevents the Council from fully exercising its primary responsibility under the Charter for the maintenance of international peace and security.

Despite this setback, France will not relent. Together with our partners, we will continue to ensure that climate and security remains firmly integrated into the Council's work, across geographical mandates, and throughout the United Nations system.
after.India:
Mr. President,

India has voted against the draft resolution.

India is second to none when it comes to climate action and climate justice. At COP26 in Glasgow, Prime Minister Narendra Modi articulated India’s vision for climate action, including our ambitious target to achieve net-zero emissions by 2070 and our vision of "Panchamrit" and Mission LiFE—Lifestyle for Environment. Our track record speaks for itself; India is among the few countries that have fulfilled and even exceeded their nationally determined contributions.

However, today’s draft resolution sought to bring the discourse on climate change into the Security Council, a body that lacks the mandate, universal representation, and specialized expertise required to address this multifaceted global challenge. 

The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and the Paris Agreement, adopted by consensus, are the primary, universal, and intergovernmental forums for negotiating and deciding upon international action on climate change. What the Council is attempting to do today is not to enhance climate action, but to undermine the multilateral architecture centered on the UNFCCC. 

Attempting to view climate change solely through the prism of peace and security risks securitizing environmental and developmental issues. There is no clear scientific or empirical consensus linking climate change directly to armed conflict. Conflicts arise from a complex interplay of historical, socioeconomic, governance, and developmental factors. Overemphasizing climate change as a driver of conflict risks obscuring the real, underlying root causes that the Council should be addressing, and could lead to simplistic and inappropriate responses.

Moreover, we are deeply concerned that bringing climate change under the Security Council's purview is an effort to evade historical responsibilities and legally binding commitments on climate finance, adaptation, and technology transfer made by developed countries under the UNFCCC. The principle of Common But Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities (CBDR-RC) is the cornerstone of global climate governance. The Security Council, dominated by a few countries and operating through non-consensual procedures, is neither equitable nor equipped to handle these issues on behalf of the entire membership, particularly developing countries.

Affording the Council a mandate over climate change would open the door to unilateral measures, selective reporting, and the imposition of conditionalities that would severely constrain the developmental prospects of developing nations. While we deeply empathize with and support our brothers and sisters in the Sahel and small island developing States, their legitimate challenges must be addressed through adequate climate finance, capacity-building, and developmental assistance—not through Council mechanisms or peacekeeping mandates.

For these reasons, India has voted against this draft resolution. We reaffirm our commitment to addressing climate change constructively through the UNFCCC framework, while ensuring that the Security Council remains focused on its primary responsibility under the UN Charter: the maintenance of international peace and security.

I thank you, Mr. President.
after.Kenya:
Kenya voted in favour of the draft resolution, and we deeply regret that the Council was unable to adopt it today. 

We thank the delegations of Niger and Ireland for their tireless, inclusive, and transparent efforts over many months to craft a balanced text that reflects the urgent realities on the ground. 

For Kenya, and indeed for our continent, the nexus between climate change and peace and security is not an academic hypothesis or a distant prospect. It is a lived, daily, and devastating reality. In the Horn of Africa, the Sahel, and the Lake Chad basin, we are witnessing unprecedented droughts, erratic rainfall, and advancing desertification. These climatic shocks decimate livelihoods, intensify competition over diminishing water and pasture, trigger forced displacements, and fuel intercommunal conflicts. Tragically, these vulnerabilities are also being exploited by terrorist and armed groups, including Al-Shabaab, to recruit, expand their influence, and undermine state authority.

This draft resolution was a modest, pragmatic, and sensible step. It did not seek to infringe upon the primary mandate of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change or the Paris Agreement, nor did it attempt to securitize global climate negotiations or duplicate the development work of other UN bodies. Rather, it sought to equip the Security Council with the necessary analytical tools, early warning mechanisms, and context-specific data to understand how climate-related security risks impact the situations already on our agenda. Conflict prevention is at the core of the Council's mandate, and ignoring one of the primary drivers and multipliers of instability directly undermines that mandate.

While the outcome of today’s vote is profoundly disappointing, a veto cannot erase the reality of climate change or its impact on international peace and security. Kenya will continue to advocate vigorously for climate security, in close partnership with the African Union and regional mechanisms, and we remain committed to ensuring that the voices of the millions of people living on the front lines of climate-induced conflict are heard and addressed by this Council.

I thank you.
after.Mexico:
Mr. President,

Mexico voted in favor of the draft resolution, which we also proudly co-sponsored alongside Niger, Ireland, and a broad cross-regional coalition of 113 Member States, representing a clear majority of the United Nations. We deeply regret that this resolution was not adopted today due to the use of the veto by a permanent member.

This outcome once again demonstrates how the use—or threat of use—of the veto paralyzes this Council and prevents it from fulfilling its Charter mandate to maintain international peace and security, running counter to the will of the overwhelming majority of the membership.

For Mexico, the link between climate change and international peace and security is not an academic abstraction; it is an undeniable reality. Extreme weather events, droughts, desertification, sea-level rise, and resource scarcity act as risk multipliers that exacerbate pre-existing vulnerabilities, trigger displacement, heighten social and economic tensions, and fuel conflict, particularly in the most fragile regions of the world.

The draft resolution presented today was a balanced, carefully calibrated text. It did not seek to duplicate or supplant the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) or the Paris Agreement, which we fully recognize as the primary forums for global climate negotiations and action. Rather, it aimed to provide the Security Council and United Nations peace operations with the analytical tools and early-warning capacity necessary to assess and address climate-related security risks, thereby strengthening our collective conflict-prevention architecture.

Ignoring the impact of climate change on international peace and security does not make it disappear. On the contrary, it limits the Council’s ability to anticipate and respond effectively to the complex drivers of modern conflict.

Despite today’s regrettable result, Mexico will continue to advocate for a comprehensive, multidimensional approach to peace and security that addresses the root causes of conflict and reflects the realities of our time.

I thank you, Mr. President.
after.Norway:
Norway deeply regrets that the Security Council was prevented from adopting this historic and necessary resolution today due to the use of the veto. 

We commend Ireland and Niger for their exemplary leadership, dedication, and inclusive consultations over many months, as well as the 113 Member States from all regions of the world who co-sponsored this draft text. The overwhelming support across the wider United Nations membership, and from 12 of the 15 members of this Council, clearly demonstrates that addressing the peace and security implications of climate change is not a distraction, but a shared global imperative.

For Norway, addressing climate-related security risks is a key priority. For millions of people around the world—particularly in vulnerable, fragile, and conflict-affected regions like the Sahel, the Lake Chad Basin, and the Horn of Africa—the links between climate shocks, environmental degradation, resource scarcity, and conflict are not a theoretical concept. They are an everyday, lived reality. Climate change acts as a threat multiplier that exacerbates vulnerabilities, drives displacement, fuels intercommunal tension, and undermines peacebuilding efforts.

This draft resolution was carefully balanced. It acknowledged the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change as the primary intergovernmental forum for negotiating the global response to climate change. At the same time, it rightly recognized that the Security Council must take responsibility for its own core mandate: the maintenance of international peace and security. To do that effectively, the Council and our peace operations must have the best available analysis, information, and tools to assess and respond to climate-related security risks on the ground.

A single veto cannot erase the reality of climate change or silence the urgent call of the international community. The Council cannot look away from the driving factors of conflict in the twenty-first century. Norway will continue to actively support efforts to integrate climate-related security risks across the Council's agenda, in our peace operations, and throughout the United Nations system.
after.Saint Vincent and the Grenadines:
Saint Vincent and the Grenadines expresses its profound disappointment that the Security Council was unable to adopt this historic draft resolution, which was co-sponsored by 113 Member States from every corner of the globe. We extend our sincere gratitude to the co-penholders, Ireland and Niger, for their tireless, inclusive, and transparent efforts throughout this process.

For Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, as a small island developing State, and for millions of people across the Sahel, the Pacific, and fragile regions worldwide, climate change is not an abstract concept or a theoretical debate. It is an existential reality and a clear and present danger. Rising sea levels, devastating extreme weather events, desertification, and ecological degradation are fundamentally reshaping the global security landscape. These climate-induced shocks exacerbate poverty, drive displacement, heighten competition over scarce resources, and act as a threat multiplier that deepens fragility and fuels conflict.

This draft resolution was a modest, balanced, and pragmatic step forward. It sought simply to equip the United Nations system and the Security Council with the necessary analytical tools, conflict-prevention strategies, and context-specific reporting to better understand and respond to climate-related security risks. It explicitly recognized the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change as the primary intergovernmental forum for negotiating the global response to climate change, reaffirmed the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities, and upheld the sovereignty and national ownership of all States. It did not infringe upon the mandates of specialized development organs; rather, it sought to ensure that our conflict-prevention and peacebuilding efforts are coherent and grounded in empirical reality.

To deny the link between climate change and international peace and security is to ignore the lived experiences of the most vulnerable peoples on our planet. While today’s veto has prevented the Council from fulfilling its Charter responsibilities on this critical matter, it cannot extinguish the overwhelming will of the international community. The momentum built here will endure. Saint Vincent and the Grenadines remains steadfast in its conviction that multilateralism must rise to the defining challenge of our time, and we will continue to advocate tirelessly for climate justice and sustainable peace.

I thank you.
after.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort:
The United Kingdom expresses its profound regret and deep disappointment at the Russian Federation’s veto of today’s draft resolution. 

This text was co-sponsored by 113 Member States from every region of the world—one of the highest numbers of co-sponsors for any Security Council resolution in history. It had the clear support of the vast majority of this Council. Yet, once again, Russia has used its veto to block the Council from fulfilling its core responsibility under the UN Charter: the maintenance of international peace and security.

The reality could not be clearer. Climate change is not an abstract concept or a distant future scenario. As we heard just last month at COP26 in Glasgow, and as leaders and communities around the world tell us daily, the adverse impacts of climate change are already here. It acts as a severe threat multiplier—aggravating existing fragilities, intensifying competition over vital resources such as water and arable land, driving displacement, and fueling conflict from the Sahel and Lake Chad to the Horn of Africa and small island developing States.

Today’s draft resolution, expertly led by Ireland and Niger, did not seek to duplicate the work of the UNFCCC, nor to supplant specialized development bodies. On the contrary, it sought to give the United Nations system, peace operations, and this Council the evidence-based tools and comprehensive analysis needed to understand and address climate-related security risks, strengthen conflict prevention, and build resilience. 

By vetoing this resolution, Russia has turned its back on the clear and urgent call of the international community, particularly the most vulnerable nations who are bearing the brunt of both climate impacts and insecurity. 

The Security Council cannot afford to be blind to the realities shaping modern conflict. Despite today’s disappointing outcome, the United Kingdom will continue to work tirelessly with our partners, within the Council and across the UN system, to ensure that the peace and security implications of climate change are properly understood, prioritized, and addressed.
after.United States of America:
The United States is deeply disappointed by the outcome of today’s vote. 

Today, a clear majority of the Security Council and more than 110 Member States from across the globe—representing diverse regions, developed and developing nations, large states and small island developing states—stood together in co-sponsoring and supporting this historic resolution. Together, we affirmed an undeniable truth: the climate crisis is a national security crisis, and it poses an existential threat to international peace and security.

Yet, by using its veto today, one permanent member—the Russian Federation—has blocked the world’s primary body responsible for international peace and security from taking a modest, sensible, and necessary step to address one of the defining challenges of our time. 

There is no justification for this veto. None whatsoever. 

This resolution was not about encroaching upon the vital work of the UNFCCC or duplicating existing environmental frameworks. It was about equipping the Security Council, United Nations peace operations, and the Secretary-General with the information and analytical tools needed to understand how climate impacts—such as historic droughts, rising sea levels, desertification, and extreme weather events—exacerbate existing fragilities, fuel conflict over scarce resources, and displace vulnerable populations, particularly in places like the Sahel, the Lake Chad Basin, and the Horn of Africa. 

By vetoing this resolution, Russia has let down the international community and turned its back on the most vulnerable countries who have repeatedly appealed to this Council for support. 

Russia may have blocked this resolution, but it cannot veto the reality of climate change. It cannot veto the lived experiences of millions of people who face insecurity every single day because of climate-induced shocks. 

The United States will continue to treat the climate crisis as the national and international security priority that it is. Alongside the overwhelming majority of the United Nations membership, we will remain steadfast in our commitment to integrating climate-related security risks into our diplomacy, conflict prevention efforts, and the Council’s work across its agenda. 

Thank you, Mr. President.
after.Viet Nam:
Viet Nam voted in favour of the draft resolution today and regrets that it could not be adopted, despite receiving broad support from the vast majority of the members of this Council and more than 110 co-sponsoring Member States.

As one of the countries most severely affected by climate change, sea-level rise, and extreme weather events, particularly in our coastal regions and the Mekong River Delta, Viet Nam is acutely aware of the existential and multifaceted threats posed by climate change. 

While climate change is fundamentally an environmental and sustainable development challenge, its adverse impacts can exacerbate socioeconomic vulnerabilities, undermine livelihoods, trigger displacement, and act as a risk multiplier that threatens peace, stability, and security, especially in fragile and conflict-affected situations.

Our support for the draft resolution is guided by several consistent principles. 

First, we reaffirm that the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and the Paris Agreement are the primary, universal, and most appropriate intergovernmental forums for addressing climate change in all its dimensions, based on the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities. The role of the Security Council must not duplicate or encroach upon the mandates of specialized UN development and environmental bodies, including the UNFCCC, the General Assembly, and the Economic and Social Council.

Second, the Security Council’s engagement on climate-related security risks must strictly adhere to its mandate under the Charter of the United Nations, focusing on context-specific, case-by-case situations on its agenda where climate factors directly threaten international peace and security.

Third, any international effort in this regard must uphold the principles of national sovereignty, territorial integrity, and political independence, and must ensure full national ownership and consultation with host countries and regional organizations. Furthermore, developed countries must fulfill their commitments to provide finance, technology transfer, and capacity-building to developing countries to build climate resilience and adaptation.

Viet Nam will continue to work constructively with all Member States and international partners to combat climate change, mitigate its adverse impacts, and promote sustainable peace and development.

I thank you.
